strengths: Rigorous theoretical framework with clear definitions distinguishing evaluability from estimability
Elegant characterization of IPM evaluability via VC and fat-shattering dimensions (Theorem 3.2 establishes strict dichotomy)
Comprehensive negative results showing Rényi/KL divergences are fundamentally unevaluable, formalizing practical perplexity failures
Well-motivated, clearly written paper with excellent presentation and honest discussion of limitations
Technically sound proofs with clever constructions for negative results
weaknesses: No empirical validation: purely theoretical with zero experiments to verify predictions on real/synthetic generative models
Limited practical impact: asymptotic sample bounds without concrete guidance; no analysis of metrics actually used in LLM evaluation (MMLU, HELM, etc.)
Incomplete results: Proposition 3.4 only establishes 3-weak evaluability for real-valued IPMs without proving optimality; multiple open questions in Section 6
Restrictive assumptions for positive results: real-valued IPMs require finite γ-fat-shattering for ALL γ ∈ (0,1/2]; Assumption 5.4 (Δ-closeness) highly constraining
Pathological constructions in negative proofs use rare events with exponentially small probability (η = e^{-(α-1)M/2}m)—practical relevance to actual model evaluation unclear
Limited scope: focused on likelihood-based metrics; ignores precision/recall, coverage, diversity metrics, benchmarks, human evaluation
Section 5 (perplexity) somewhat disconnected from main narrative; results require very strong assumptions or don't apply to intended metrics

strengths: Addresses fundamental problem of when generative model evaluation metrics can be reliably estimated from finite samples, with compelling practical motivations
Introduces a precise mathematical framework for evaluability (strong vs. weak) that enables rigorous analysis of metric properties

Provides complete and elegant characterization of IPM evaluability with tight bounds: finite VC dimension yields strong evaluability, infinite VC yields 3-weak evaluability with proven optimality of factor-3
Establishes strong negative results showing α-Rényi and KL divergences are fundamentally not evaluable due to dependence on rare events
Provides theoretical justification for known perplexity failures and identifies conditions under which it succeeds, connecting empirical observations to formal theory
Technically sound throughout with complete proofs; uses appropriate tools from statistical learning theory (VC dimension, fat-shattering dimension, concentration inequalities)
Well-written with clear motivation, logical progression, and effective use of summary tables
Honest discussion of limitations and open questions, avoiding overclaiming
weaknesses: Limited practical applicability: assumes access to ground truth distribution q* and IID samples, which do not hold when evaluating pre-trained models; gap between theory (probability distributions) and practice (neural networks) not adequately addressed

Incomplete results: Proposition 3.4 for real-valued IPMs only achieves 3-weak evaluability for unbounded fat-shattering case, not mirroring the strict dichotomy of Theorem 3.2; authors acknowledge as open question but weakens contribution
Negative results lack constructive alternatives: no guidance on which metrics practitioners should use instead, or how to modify problematic metrics for evaluability
Lower bounds for Rényi divergences rely on pathological constructions with exponentially rare events (η = e^{-(α-1)M/2}) that may not reflect realistic distributions; unclear if results generalize
Coverage Profile section (4.2) appears disconnected from main narrative; metric from 2025 paper with restrictive margin assumptions suggests this may be incomplete work

Substantial open questions remain (Section 6): relationship between estimability and strong evaluability, strict dichotomy for real-valued IPMs, general evaluability of β-restricted KL, reducing perceived completeness
No experimental validation: entirely theory-focused with no empirical verification of predictions on real models or datasets
Limited metric coverage: focuses narrowly on IPMs and Rényi divergences; other common metrics (BLEU, ROUGE) not discussed; Hellinger distance relegated to footnote
Sample complexity analysis incomplete: bounds depend on ε, δ but practical interpretation unclear; no comparison to practice or discussion of constants
Proposition 5.6's assumption of ∆-closeness essentially requires candidate model near truth, limiting practical applicability despite being presented as positive result

strengths: Addresses a fundamental and timely problem in generative model evaluation with rigorous mathematical framework
Elegant and comprehensive theoretical results, particularly the tight dichotomy for binary IPMs (Theorem 3.2) and the striking negative results for Rényi/KL divergences
Well-structured paper with clear progression and excellent Table 1 summary; generally clear writing despite technical density
Provides actionable insights for practitioners: guides away from perplexity for certain metrics, shows fundamental limitations of KL-based evaluation
Technically sound proofs with appropriate connection to learning theory (VC dimension, fat-shattering dimension, uniform convergence)
Clearly identifies open theoretical questions and acknowledges limitations (e.g., real-valued IPM case)
Comprehensive coverage of multiple metric classes and scoring functions with formal definitions of strong vs. weak evaluability
weaknesses: Complete absence of empirical validation or experiments—even toy examples would ground theory in practice and show practical sample complexity constants
Incomplete characterization for real-valued IPMs (Proposition 3.4): cannot prove 3-factor is optimal, leaving a theoretical gap that mirrors the binary case
Limited practical guidance: identifies what practitioners shouldn't do but provides limited guidance on metric design or what they should use instead
Restrictive assumptions in positive results (Theorem 4.8 margin assumption, Proposition 5.6 ∆-closeness requirement) that reduce scope compared to negative results
Perplexity counterexamples are somewhat artificial (3-point supports)—no discussion of whether these pathological cases arise in practice
Limited engagement with finite-support and finite-sample behavior; framework is asymptotic with hidden constants in complexity bounds
Theorem 3.6 (finite taxonomy) is tangential to core evaluability narrative and disrupts flow; relevance to practitioners unclear
